info.bio:
Hank Ballard (November 18, 1927 – March 2, 2003) was an American rhythm and blues singer and a member of the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame. He was the lead vocalist of the group Hank Ballard & the Midnighters.

He was born in Detroit, Michigan but grew up in Bessemer, Alabama, where he sang in church.

In 1951, Ballard moved back to Detroit and formed a doo wop group. He soon joined a group called The Royals, along with Henry Booth, Charles Sutton, Sonny Woods and Alonzo Tucker.

scenes.book: Heavy Metal: The Music and Its Culture
scenes.author: Deena Weinstein
scenes.desc: El Parents Music Resource Center, fundado por esposas de políticos de Washington, lleva en 1985 la «música obscena» al Senado de Estados Unidos en las audiencias sobre el etiquetado de discos. Allí el musicólogo Joe Stuessy, asesor del PMRC, declara que el heavy actual es categóricamente distinto de toda música popular anterior porque contiene odio, y el senador Albert Gore pregunta por la tendencia a la violencia explícita, el sexo y el sadomasoquismo «en el área del heavy metal». Para Weinstein es el ejemplo de cómo el género se convierte en asunto público sin que nadie sepa de qué está hablando.

podcast.title: Decline by 1958
podcast.body: By 1958, Hank Ballard and the Midnighters were largely a forgotten group. Their R&B style, rooted in the LA sound pioneered by Johnny Otis, had been superseded by newer sounds from Memphis, Chicago, and New York. They had not had a hit in three years and were concerned about being dropped by their record label. "By 1958 though, they were largely a forgotten group."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Dick Clark's Reasons for Exclusion
podcast.body: Dick Clark deliberately did not invite Hank Ballard and the Midnighters onto his shows to perform "The Twist," even as it began to chart. Various reasons are cited: they might have been too busy touring, Clark preferred someone "less threatening" (understood to mean "less obviously Black"), someone younger, concerns about the "adult nature" of Ballard's act, or Clark's preference for performers with whom he had a financial link. "Now, there were several stories about why Clark didn't ask Hank Ballard and the Midnighters onto the show."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Discovery of "The Twist"
podcast.body: Despite their decline in chart success, the group remained a popular live act and toured regularly. While performing in Florida (either Tampa or Miami), they played on the same bill as the gospel group the Sensational Nightingales, who offered them the secular song "The Twist" as they could not perform it themselves. "But they were still a popular ally of Act, and they were touring regularly, and in Florida, some sources say they were in Tampa or there's Miami. They happened to play on the same bill as a gospel group called the Sensational Nightingales."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Guitarist Cal Green's Imprisonment
podcast.body: Cal Green, the Midnighters' guitarist who helped adapt "The Twist" melody, ended up in prison for two years around this time due to marijuana possession. This meant he missed out on almost the entire story of "The Twist" craze and its subsequent success. "Green, who ended up in prison for two years from marijuana possession around this time, and missed out on almost all of this story."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Influence on The Famous Flames' Style
podcast.body: Hank Ballard and the Midnighters were one of two groups that The Famous Flames increasingly patterned their style after. Their work, particularly with its "blatant sexuality" in "Work With Me Annie," contributed to the Famous Flames' focus on energy and raw, visceral emotion. "Hank Ballad and the Midnighters, whose work with me Annie had had for the time a blatant sexuality that was unusual in successful records."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Perennial Background Player
podcast.body: The group was noted as a "perennial background player" in the history of rock music, having been discussed in the episode on "The Wallflower" and mentioned in passing in the episode on Jackie Wilson. "One of the groups that have been a perennial background player in our story so far has been Hank Ballard in the Midnighters."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Reissue with Overdubbed Saxophone
podcast.body: Upon hearing Chubby Checker's version of "The Twist," which sounded nearly identical to his own, King Records swiftly brought a saxophone player into the studio. They overdubbed an identical saxophone part onto Ballard's original track and reissued it to make it sound even more like Checker's successful sound-alike. "King Records quickly got a saxophone player into the studio to overdub an identical part on Ballard's track and reissue it, to make it sound more like the sound alike."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
